title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 53)
hook: despised, bruised for our sins, and by his bruises healed; read on Good Friday

segments.voice: Yesterday, comfort ye, and the promise that the weary will walk and not faint. Your line was comfort, my people. Who did you send your tender sentence to? Day four hundred twenty, the end of week sixty.

A man is riding home in a chariot on a desert road, reading aloud from a scroll of Isaiah. He's an official of the queen of Ethiopia, a long way from home after worshiping in Jerusalem. That's in the Acts of the Apostles. A follower of Jesus named Philip runs up alongside and asks: do you understand what you're reading? And the man says: how can I, unless someone guides me? Then he asks the question readers still ask about this chapter: of whom is the prophet saying this? Of himself, or of someone else? The passage he was reading is today's word.
screen: `A CHARIOT ON A DESERT ROAD.` → `DO YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU READ?` → `OF WHOM DOES THE PROPHET SPEAK?`

segments.voice: Isaiah's later chapters sing of a figure called the servant of the Lord, and in chapter fifty-three the servant suffers. The Douay-Rheims: "Despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity." People turned their faces from him and thought God had struck him. And then the voice in the poem realizes what was really happening: "he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins: the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed." We thought he was being punished for his own wrongs. He was carrying ours. "All we like sheep have gone astray." And the servant doesn't fight back: like a lamb led to the slaughter, he opens not his mouth. Who is he? Readers have answered in different ways, and it's worth knowing who says what. Jewish tradition has often read the servant as the people of Israel, suffering among the nations, and some ancient Jewish readers saw a coming Messiah. Christians, from the earliest days Acts records, have read it as Jesus. In Acts, Philip begins from this very passage and tells the Ethiopian about Jesus, and the man asks to be baptized at the next stream. The Catholic Church reads Isaiah fifty-three every Good Friday, as the first reading before the Passion: the man of sorrows, the lamb who was silent, healing through wounds. And that's week sixty: exile, Isaiah's here am I, Emmanuel, ploughshares, the wolf and the lamb, comfort, and the servant who carried what wasn't his.
screen: `A MAN OF SORROWS.` · `WE THOUGHT GOD STRUCK HIM.` · `ISRAEL, OR THE MESSIAH?` · `READ EVERY GOOD FRIDAY.` · then, large: `BY HIS BRUISES WE ARE HEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who suffers unjustly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone carrying a weight they didn't earn. A child in a hard home. Someone wrongly accused. A person blamed for a family's troubles. Someone sick because of where they live. Picture them the way the poem pictures the servant: people looking away. Don't look away. Hold their face in your mind. If you pray, you can bring them before God, and ask that they be seen and healed. If you don't, simply refuse, for these minutes, to turn your face from them. The bell holds the time.
The suffering servant. Isaiah's figure who is despised, bears the sins of others, and by whose bruises we are healed; the Church reads him as Christ. Today's word.
Your line: by his bruises. Today, take one burden off someone who's carrying more than their share, even something small. Day four hundred twenty.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophecy about the crucifixion, written in advance.
what it means: a poem about a servant who is despised and silent, and whose suffering heals others. Christians read it as Christ; Jewish tradition often as Israel.
what a scholar hears: scholars count this as the fourth of Isaiah's servant songs, running from 52:13; Acts 8 shows Christians reading it of Jesus from the earliest days.
